Visa Approval Facilitation

Problem Statement¶

Context:¶

Business communities in the United States are facing high demand for human resources, but one of the constant challenges is identifying and attracting the right talent, which is perhaps the most important element in remaining competitive. Companies in the United States look for hard-working, talented, and qualified individuals both locally as well as abroad.

The Immigration and Nationality Act (INA) of the US permits foreign workers to come to the United States to work on either a temporary or permanent basis. The act also protects US workers against adverse impacts on their wages or working conditions by ensuring US employers' compliance with statutory requirements when they hire foreign workers to fill workforce shortages. The immigration programs are administered by the Office of Foreign Labor Certification (OFLC).

OFLC processes job certification applications for employers seeking to bring foreign workers into the United States and grants certifications in those cases where employers can demonstrate that there are not sufficient US workers available to perform the work at wages that meet or exceed the wage paid for the occupation in the area of intended employment.

Objective:¶

In FY 2016, the OFLC processed 775,979 employer applications for 1,699,957 positions for temporary and permanent labor certifications. This was a nine percent increase in the overall number of processed applications from the previous year. The process of reviewing every case is becoming a tedious task as the number of applicants is increasing every year.

The increasing number of applicants every year calls for a Machine Learning based solution that can help in shortlisting the candidates having higher chances of VISA approval. OFLC has hired the firm EasyVisa for data-driven solutions. You as a data scientist at EasyVisa have to analyze the data provided and, with the help of a classification model:

  • Facilitate the process of visa approvals.
  • Recommend a suitable profile for the applicants for whom the visa should be certified or denied based on the drivers that significantly influence the case status.

Data Description¶

The data contains the different attributes of employee and the employer. The detailed data dictionary is given below.

  • case_id: ID of each visa application
  • continent: Information of continent the employee
  • education_of_employee: Information of education of the employee
  • has_job_experience: Does the employee has any job experience? Y= Yes; N = No
  • requires_job_training: Does the employee require any job training? Y = Yes; N = No
  • no_of_employees: Number of employees in the employer's company
  • yr_of_estab: Year in which the employer's company was established
  • region_of_employment: Information of foreign worker's intended region of employment in the US.
  • prevailing_wage: Average wage paid to similarly employed workers in a specific occupation in the area of intended employment. The purpose of the prevailing wage is to ensure that the foreign worker is not underpaid compared to other workers offering the same or similar service in the same area of employment.
  • unit_of_wage: Unit of prevailing wage. Values include Hourly, Weekly, Monthly, and Yearly.
  • full_time_position: Is the position of work full-time? Y = Full Time Position; N = Part Time Position
  • case_status: Flag indicating if the Visa was certified or denied

  • Data quality issue are present in the data. 'no_of_employees' and 'prevailing_wage' attributes need to be revisited for cleansing.

  • Some of the categorical attributes are heavily skewed and may influence model performance

  • High variance is observed and could be due to outliers or wider range of values.

  • Dominent categories are present within some attributes. examples: 'Asia' for continent, 'Bachelor's' for education.

#Function to plot both histogram and boxplot

def histogram_boxplot(data, feature, figsize=(15, 10), kde=False, bins=None):
    """
    Boxplot and histogram combined

    data: dataframe
    feature: dataframe column
    figsize: size of figure (default (15,10))
    kde: whether to show the density curve (default False)
    bins: number of bins for histogram (default None)
    """
    f2, (ax_box2, ax_hist2) = plt.subplots(
        nrows=2,  # Number of rows of the subplot grid= 2
        sharex=True,  # x-axis will be shared among all subplots
        gridspec_kw={"height_ratios": (0.25, 0.75)},
        figsize=figsize,
    )  # creating the 2 subplots
    sns.boxplot(
        data=data, x=feature, ax=ax_box2, showmeans=True, color="violet"
    )  # boxplot will be created and a triangle will indicate the mean value of the column
    sns.histplot(
        data=data, x=feature, kde=True, ax=ax_hist2, bins=bins
    ) if bins else sns.histplot(
        data=data, x=feature, kde=True, ax=ax_hist2
    )  # For histogram

    # Calculate and plot mean and median only if the feature is numeric
    if pd.api.types.is_numeric_dtype(data[feature]):
      ax_hist2.axvline(
          data[feature].mean(), color="green", linestyle="--"
      )  # Add mean to the histogram
      ax_hist2.axvline(
          data[feature].median(), color="blue", linestyle="-"
      )  # Add median to the histogram
    else:
      #add mode
      ax_hist2.axvline(
          data[feature].mode()[0], color="blue", linestyle="-"
      )
In [25]:
# function to create labeled barplots


def labeled_barplot(data, feature, perc=False, n=None):
    """
    Barplot with percentage at the top

    data: dataframe
    feature: dataframe column
    perc: whether to display percentages instead of count (default is False)
    n: displays the top n category levels (default is None, i.e., display all levels)
    """

    total = len(data[feature])  # length of the column
    count = data[feature].nunique()
    if n is None:
        plt.figure(figsize=(count + 2, 6))
    else:
        plt.figure(figsize=(n + 2, 6))

    plt.xticks(rotation=90, fontsize=15)
    ax = sns.countplot(
        data=data,
        x=feature,
        palette="Paired",
        order=data[feature].value_counts().index[:n],
    )

    for p in ax.patches:
        if perc == True:
            label = "{:.1f}%".format(
                100 * p.get_height() / total
            )  # percentage of each class of the category
        else:
            label = p.get_height()  # count of each level of the category

        x = p.get_x() + p.get_width() / 2  # width of the plot
        y = p.get_height()  # height of the plot

        ax.annotate(
            label,
            (x, y),
            ha="center",
            va="center",
            size=12,
            xytext=(0, 5),
            textcoords="offset points",
        )  # annotate the percentage

    plt.show()  # show the plot

### function to plot distributions wrt target


def distribution_plot_wrt_target(data, predictor, target):

    fig, axs = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(12, 10))

    target_uniq = data[target].unique()

    axs[0, 0].set_title("Distribution of target for target=" + str(target_uniq[0]))
    sns.histplot(
        data=data[data[target] == target_uniq[0]],
        x=predictor,
        kde=True,
        ax=axs[0, 0],
        color="teal",
        stat="density",
    )

    axs[0, 1].set_title("Distribution of target for target=" + str(target_uniq[1]))
    sns.histplot(
        data=data[data[target] == target_uniq[1]],
        x=predictor,
        kde=True,
        ax=axs[0, 1],
        color="orange",
        stat="density",
    )

    axs[1, 0].set_title("Boxplot w.r.t target")
    sns.boxplot(data=data, x=target, y=predictor, ax=axs[1, 0], palette="gist_rainbow")

    axs[1, 1].set_title("Boxplot (without outliers) w.r.t target")
    sns.boxplot(
        data=data,
        x=target,
        y=predictor,
        ax=axs[1, 1],
        showfliers=False,
        palette="gist_rainbow",
    )

    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

def distribution_boxplot_wrt_target(data, predictor, target):

    fig, axs = plt.subplots(1,2 , figsize=(12, 5))

    sns.boxplot(data=data, x=target, y=predictor, ax=axs[0], palette="gist_rainbow")

    sns.boxplot(
        data=data,
        x=target,
        y=predictor,
        ax=axs[1],
        showfliers=False,
        palette="gist_rainbow",
    )

    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

def stacked_barplot(data, predictor, target):
    """
    Print the category counts and plot a stacked bar chart

    data: dataframe
    predictor: independent variable
    target: target variable
    """
    count = data[predictor].nunique()
    sorter = data[target].value_counts().index[-1]
    tab1 = pd.crosstab(data[predictor], data[target], margins=True).sort_values(
        by=sorter, ascending=False
    )
    print(tab1)
    print("-" * 120)
    tab = pd.crosstab(data[predictor], data[target], normalize="index").sort_values(
        by=sorter, ascending=False
    )
    tab.plot(kind="bar", stacked=True, figsize=(count + 5, 5))
    plt.legend(
        loc="lower left", frameon=False,
    )
    plt.legend(loc="upper left", bbox_to_anchor=(1, 1))
    plt.show()

Model Building¶

Model Evaluation Criterion¶

Model Evaluation Criterion: F1-Score

The best evaluation metric for this problem is the F1-score because:

  1. Both False Positives (FP) and False Negatives (FN) are critical
* **False Positive (FP)**: A visa is wrongly certified when it should be denied → Leads to hiring an ineligible employee, which may violate regulations and impact U.S. workers.
* **False Negative (FN)**: A visa is wrongly denied when it should be certified → Leads to losing a skilled worker who could contribute to the economy.
  1. Class Imbalance is Likely:
* Visa approvals (certified cases) are higher than denials, meaning the dataset is imbalanced.
* Accuracy is not a good metric in such cases because a model predicting mostly "Certified" would still appear highly accurate.
* **F1-score** balances Precision (minimizing FP) and Recall (minimizing FN), ensuring fair consideration of both error types.
  1. Regulatory and Business Impact Considerations:
* A visa approval system must be fair and reliable, avoiding bias in decision-making.
* Using balanced class weights helps to ensure equal focus on both certified and denied cases.

Additional Considerations

  • Precision vs Recall Tradeoff:
    • If avoiding false approvals is more important (to prevent unqualified hires), Precision should be prioritized.
    • If avoiding false denials is more important (to prevent losing skilled workers), Recall should be prioritized.
    • Since both errors are equally important, F1-score (harmonic mean of Precision & Recall) is the best measure.

Let's define a function to output different metrics (including recall) on the train and test set and a function to show confusion matrix so that we do not have to use the same code repetitively while evaluating models.

In [54]:
# defining a function to compute different metrics to check performance of a classification model built using sklearn


def model_performance_classification_sklearn(model, predictors, target):
    """
    Function to compute different metrics to check classification model performance

    model: classifier
    predictors: independent variables
    target: dependent variable
    """

    # predicting using the independent variables
    pred = model.predict(predictors)

    acc = accuracy_score(target, pred)  # to compute Accuracy
    recall = recall_score(target, pred)  # to compute Recall
    precision = precision_score(target, pred)  # to compute Precision
    f1 = f1_score(target, pred)  # to compute F1-score

    # creating a dataframe of metrics
    df_perf = pd.DataFrame(
        {"Accuracy": acc, "Recall": recall, "Precision": precision, "F1": f1,},
        index=[0],
    )

    return df_perf
In [55]:
def confusion_matrix_sklearn(model, predictors, target):
    """
    To plot the confusion_matrix with percentages

    model: classifier
    predictors: independent variables
    target: dependent variable
    """
    y_pred = model.predict(predictors)
    cm = confusion_matrix(target, y_pred)
    labels = np.asarray(
        [
            ["{0:0.0f}".format(item) + "\n{0:.2%}".format(item / cm.flatten().sum())]
            for item in cm.flatten()
        ]
    ).reshape(2, 2)

    plt.figure(figsize=(6, 4))
    sns.heatmap(cm, annot=labels, fmt="")
    plt.ylabel("True label")
    plt.xlabel("Predicted label")

Model building function¶

In [57]:
# This function can be used for evaluating original data, oversampled data and undersampled data

def evaluate_models(models, X_train, y_train, X_val, y_val, data_label):
    results = []

    for name, model in models:
        # Train model
        model.fit(X_train, y_train)

        # Predictions
        y_train_pred = model.predict(X_train)
        y_val_pred = model.predict(X_val)

        # Compute Training Metrics
        train_acc = accuracy_score(y_train, y_train_pred)
        train_recall = recall_score(y_train, y_train_pred)
        train_precision = precision_score(y_train, y_train_pred)
        train_f1 = f1_score(y_train, y_train_pred)

        # Compute Validation Metrics
        val_acc = accuracy_score(y_val, y_val_pred)
        val_recall = recall_score(y_val, y_val_pred)
        val_precision = precision_score(y_val, y_val_pred)
        val_f1 = f1_score(y_val, y_val_pred)

        # Append results
        results.append([
            data_label, name,
            round(train_acc, 4), round(train_recall, 4), round(train_precision, 4), round(train_f1, 4),
            round(val_acc, 4), round(val_recall, 4), round(val_precision, 4), round(val_f1, 4)
        ])

    return results

  1. Bagging, Random Forest, and Decision Tree (dtree) show signs of overfitting:
  • Their training accuracy, recall, precision, and F1 scores are nearly perfect (1.000), indicating that they memorized the training data.
  • However, their validation performance is much lower, suggesting that they fail to generalize well to new data.
  1. GBM (Gradient Boosting), Adaboost and XGBoost seem to generalize better:

  • They do not overfit as much.

  • Validation and training scores are closer.

  • These models may be more robust and are likely better choices.

  • For Overfitting Models (Bagging, Random Forest, Decision Tree):

    • We could apply hyperparameter tuning: Reduce tree depth, increase min samples per leaf, add regularization.
    • Use feature selection to remove irrelevant/noisy features.
    • Increase data with data augmentation or synthetic data generation if possible.

  • For GBM, Adaboost and XGBoost (Best Models):

    • We could consider hyperparameter tuning for a slight boost.
    • If recall is crucial, GBM or Adaboost is better.
    • If balance (F1 score) is needed, GBM, Adaboost or XGBoost are better.

If we focus only on the F1 score then:

  • Best Model: AdaBoost (0.820, No Overfitting)
  • Runner-Up: GBM (0.830 -> 0.824, Minimal Overfitting)
  • XGBoost is a Solid Alternative (0.893 -> 0.810)
    • If optimized further, it could outperform GBM and AdaBoost.
  • Avoid Using Decision Tree & Bagging
    • These models overfit too much, leading to unreliable predictions on new data.

If optimized further, it could outperform GBM and AdaBoost. Avoid Using Decision Tree & Bagging These models overfit too much, leading to unreliable predictions on new data.

Was oversampling beneficial?¶

Pros of Oversampling:

Slightly improved recall for some models (GBM, AdaBoost). XGBoost maintained precision well, meaning false positives were controlled. Cons of Oversampling:

Validation performance slightly dropped across all models—suggesting oversampling added noise. Overfitting was not reduced for Decision Tree & Random Forest—they still memorized the training set. Slight drop in precision, leading to more false positives in some models.

Was Undersampling Beneficial?¶

  • Pros of Undersampling:

    • Increased precision for most models (better confidence in positive predictions).
    • Lower memory and computational requirements—useful for large datasets.
    • GBM and AdaBoost handled undersampling better than other models.

  • Cons of Undersampling:

    • Significantly reduced recall—higher false negatives across all models.
    • Lower validation accuracy and F1-score for all models.
    • Random Forest & Decision Tree overfitting was not solved, and they performed worse.

Hyperparameter Tuning¶

  • We will tune AdaBoost, GBM and XGBoost due to their performance described/plotted above.
  • We will also use oversampled data as the model performance drops significantly with undersampling.

Observations After Hyperparameter Tuning and Stacking

  • Overfitting Risk:

    • Tuned XGBoost and Tuned Gradient Boosting have the largest accuracy drops (0.084 & 0.077), indicating possible overfitting.
    • Stacking Classifier has the lowest accuracy drop (0.019), meaning it generalizes slightly better in terms of accuracy.
    • Tuned AdaBoost shows an improved recall drop (0.005), indicating strong stability in identifying positive cases.

  • Recall vs Precision:

    • Tuned XGBoost and Stacking Classifier prioritize recall over precision, meaning they are better for detecting as many true positives as possible but at the cost of more false positives.
    • Tuned AdaBoost and GBM maintain a better balance between recall and precision.
    • Tuned GBM has the best balance (smallest recall-precision difference of 0.086).

  • F1-score:

    • Our focus has been mainly on the F1-score (as decided previously)
    • Tuned XGBoost has the highest F1-score (0.822), indicating strong overall performance.
    • Tuned GBM is just slightly behind (0.819), making it another excellent choice.
    • Tuned AdaBoost is also very close (0.818).
    • Stacking Classifier has the lowest F1-score (0.815) but is still competitive.

Conclusion about models

  • XGBoost with hyperparameter tuning & oversampling has very low overfitting and indicates great generalization and is the best choice based purely on F1 score stability.
  • This being said - GBM with hyperparameter tuning & oversampling is also a strong candidate.
  • There is a third candidate AdaBoost with original data. This too performed well without the need for tuning but fell slightly behind.

Next Steps

  • We want to select a model that performs/generalizes well on unseen data (test data). This would mean relatively close but high performance between training, validation and test data sets (while avoiding overfitting).
  • It is once again important to remember that evaluation is based on F1-scores as decided previously.

# Loop through models and plot confusion matrices with percentages
for ax, (model, title) in zip(axes, models):
    y_pred = model.predict(X_test)
    cm = confusion_matrix(y_test, y_pred)

    # Normalize the confusion matrix to show percentages
    cm_percent = cm.astype('float') / cm.sum() * 100

    # Format labels with absolute counts and percentages
    labels = np.asarray([
        [f"{count}\n{percent:.2f}%" for count, percent in zip(cm.flatten(), cm_percent.flatten())]
    ]).reshape(cm.shape)

    # Plot using seaborn heatmap
    sns.heatmap(cm, annot=labels, fmt="", cmap="Blues", ax=ax)
    ax.set_ylabel("True Label")
    ax.set_xlabel("Predicted Label")
    ax.set_title(title)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Observations on performance of Tuned XGBoost model on the test data set

The Tuned XGBoost model, optimized using hyperparameter tuning and oversampling, demonstrates strong generalization across datasets.

  • F1 score (0.822 -> 0.817) and Recall (0.9560 -> 0.945) showing a slight decline, suggesting minimal overfitting and good retention of prediction performance.

  • Precision is stable (0.722 -> 0.719) remains stable, indicating consitent balance between false positives and false negatives.

  • The top three most influential factors for application certification are Education of employee, Job experience, and Region of employment —highlighting the critical attributes driving model predictions.

  • Overall, the Tuned XGBoost model generalizes well and retains its predictive strength across unseen test data, making it a strong candidate for production deployment.

Actionable Insights and Recommendations¶

Final Model Selection & Caveats

  • We prioritized F1-score as the key metric, ensuring a balanced trade-off between precision and recall to handle class imbalances effectively.

  • A strong generalization capability was essential— we wanted models with consistently high but close performance across training, validation, and test datasets, avoiding overfitting.

  • Undersampling was ruled out due to performance drops, making it unsuitable for production use.

  • The top three candidates based on performance were:

    • Tuned XGBoost (Highest F1-score, strong recall, slightly lower precision).
    • Tuned GBM (Very close performance to XGBoost, slightly better balance)
    • Tuned AdaBoost (Excellent generalization, least overfitting).

  • Tuned XGBoost emerged as the best choice, achieving the highest F1-score on unseen/test data, with strong recall and slightly lower precision.

  • Final production model considerations:

    • Cost of false positives vs. false negatives should be analyzed before deployment.

    • Implementation complexity of each model should be factored into the decision.

Final Pick: Tuned XGBoost (with further validation based on business impact of false positives/negatives).

Key Drivers of Visa Approvals:

  • Education Level: Higher education levels, particularly Doctorate and Master's degrees, significantly increase the chances of visa approval.

  • Job Experience: Applicants with prior job experience have a considerably higher approval rate compared to those without experience.

  • Region of Employment: While not identified as a primary driver in the initial analysis, the feature importance plots suggest that the region of employment might have a stronger influence than previously thought.

  • Continent: Europe and Africa have the highest visa certification rates, while Asia has a significant number of applications but also a higher denial rate.

  • Prevailing Wage: While not a primary factor, higher prevailing wages generally correlate with better chances of approval, although outliers exist in both approved and denied cases.

Recommendations:

  • Prioritize Applications: Focus on processing applications from individuals with higher education levels (Doctorate, Master's), relevant job experience, and annual salary offers. This can expedite the approval process for the most promising candidates.

  • Targeted Outreach: Conduct targeted outreach programs in countries or regions with lower approval rates (example: Asia) to educate potential applicants on factors that influence visa success. Emphasize the importance of relevant education and job experience.

  • Employer Collaboration: Partner with employers to encourage them to offer competitive salaries and long-term employment opportunities, which are more likely to result in visa certification.

  • Case Review: Implement a more thorough review process for applications with lower-paying or hourly wage jobs, as these have a higher risk of denial. Ensure that employer details and job descriptions are carefully evaluated.

  • Data-Driven Decisions: Continue to refine the prediction model with updated data and consider incorporating additional factors that may influence visa decisions. Regularly evaluate the model's performance to ensure accuracy and fairness.

  • Transparency: Make information about the key factors driving visa approval accessible to potential applicants to promote transparency and encourage qualified candidates to apply.
